Dopemux false-positive filtering instructions

Use these filters after producing candidate findings. Keep true positives even
when they appear in noisy areas, but require a clear runtime or operator-impact
path before reporting.

Report a candidate finding when at least one is true
- It is reachable from compose.yml, an active Dockerfile, an active package
  entrypoint, an active GitHub Actions workflow, or documented startup commands.
- It affects an exposed HTTP, WebSocket, SSE, webhook, MCP, CLI, or automation
  surface.
- It can modify or disclose PM state, workflow transitions, ConPort context,
  dope-memory chronicles, indexed code/docs, event streams, provider API keys,
  local workspace files, host-mounted data, or generated proof artifacts.
- It can weaken authentication, authorization, signature verification, replay
  protection, CORS isolation, process execution safety, or host/container
  boundaries.
- It is in code copied into a runtime image even if the exact endpoint is not
  currently wired.

Suppress or downgrade a candidate finding when all are true
- The vulnerable-looking code is only in tests, simulator tests, generated
  reports, archived material, backup compose files, examples, or fixture data.
- There is no active import, package entrypoint, compose service, CI path,
  Docker COPY path, or documented operator path to the code.
- The value is an obvious placeholder such as example.com, changeme, dummy,
  fake, test-only, or redacted text and is not used as a runtime default.

Common repo-specific noise
- docker/mcp-servers-source/pal/pal-mcp-server/simulator_tests contains
  intentional vulnerable examples for security tool validation.
- tests, service-local test_* files, generated reports, proof artifacts, and
  extraction outputs can contain historical or synthetic vulnerability text.
- Archived, backup, and legacy compose files can show old Docker socket mounts,
  host networking, or permissive mounts. Report only if an active workflow or
  operator command still uses them.
- Documentation may mention old service ports or stale architecture. Treat this
  as documentation drift unless the stale value causes an exploitable runtime
  path.

Do not suppress these without proof
- Default runtime credentials in compose.yml or active service config.
- Missing auth on endpoints that mutate workflow, PM, memory, event, retrieval,
  bridge, or local workspace state.
- Credentialed wildcard CORS on active services.
- Webhook signature verification or replay/deduplication defects.
- Arbitrary file access through user-controlled workspace, relative path,
  transcript path, archive path, or retrieval parameters.
- Shell command injection, unsafe subprocess execution, or untrusted environment
  propagation in active CLI/service code.
- Unsafe deserialization in active memory, cache, checkpoint, or session flows.
- Writable host mounts or Docker socket exposure in active compose/runtime paths.

How to phrase retained findings
- Lead with the affected service and reachable entrypoint.
- Include exact file and line references.
- Explain the authority boundary crossed, if any.
- State why the code is active or plausibly active.
- State exploit prerequisites and impact.
- Recommend the smallest fail-closed mitigation.

If runtime authority is unclear
- Mark the finding as "needs runtime confirmation" instead of suppressing it
  when the issue is security-significant and the code is copied into images or
  reachable through an active package path.
- Mark pure architecture drift separately from exploitable vulnerabilities.
